claim: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second-highest cause of cancer-related mortality.
source: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second-highest cause of cancer-related mortality (Siegel et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2023

claim: Radiotherapy is crucial for CRC management, especially in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (cT3-4N+).
source: Radiotherapy is crucial for CRC management, especially in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (cT3-4N+) (Glynne-Jones et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Glynne-Jones et al., 2017

claim: Neoadjuvant therapies show clinical or pathological complete response in 16–30% of patients.
source: Neoadjuvant therapies show clinical or pathological complete response in 16–30% of patients, realising downstaging in approximately 60% of patients, significantly enhancing local control, and facilitating curative surgery (Cercek et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cercek et al., 2018

claim: Neoadjuvant therapies realize downstaging in approximately 60% of patients.
source: Neoadjuvant therapies show clinical or pathological complete response in 16–30% of patients, realising downstaging in approximately 60% of patients, significantly enhancing local control, and facilitating curative surgery (Cercek et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cercek et al., 2018

claim: Radiotherapy is beneficial in initially unresectable and recurrent cases with limited metastasis to organs, such as the liver and lungs.
source: Moreover, radiotherapy is beneficial in initially unresectable and recurrent cases with limited metastasis to organs, such as the liver and lungs (Cervantes et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cervantes et al., 2023

claim: Within mitochondria, 90% of cellular ROS are generated by complexes I, II, and IV of the electron transport chain.
source: Within mitochondria, 90% of cellular ROS are generated by complexes I, II, and IV of the electron transport chain (Glasauer and Chandel, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Glasauer and Chandel, 2014

claim: Radiation ionises water molecules, creating an intracellular surge of ROS, which indirectly cause two-thirds of DNA damage.
source: Radiation ionises water molecules, creating an intracellular surge of ROS, which indirectly cause two-thirds of DNA damage (Chio and Tuveson, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chio and Tuveson, 2017

claim: CPT1A is absent in several tumours.
source: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT1) is an outer mitochondrial membrane that catalyses the rate-limiting step of fatty acid oxidation and is absent in several tumours (Melone et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Melone et al., 2018

claim: CPT1A mRNA levels were lower in CRC tissues compared to adjacent non-tumour tissues in six GEO microarrays.
source: Analysis of CRC mRNA sequencing arrays from GEO consistently indicated low CPT1A mRNA levels in CRC (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by data from GEO microarray analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: CPT1A transcript levels were lower in most colon cancers (19/24 pairs) than in the adjacent non-tumour tissues.
source: The transcript levels of CPT1A were lower in most colon cancers (19/24 pairs) than in the adjacent non-tumour tissues (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B

claim: CPT1A protein levels were lower in most CRC tissues (14/16 pairs) than in the adjacent non-tumour tissues.
source: Meanwhile, CPT1A protein levels were lower in most CRC tissues (14/16 pairs) than in the adjacent non-tumour tissues (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1C

claim: CPT1A mRNA levels were significantly lower in colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) tissues than in the adjacent non-tumour tissues.
source: Further exploration of CPT1A expression in TCGA revealed that CPT1A mRNA levels were significantly lower in colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) tissues than in the adjacent non-tumour tissues (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: CPT1A mRNA levels were significantly lower in rectal adenocarcinoma (READ) tissues than in the adjacent non-tumour tissues.
source: Similar results were observed for rectal adenocarcinoma (READ) (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1E

claim: CPT1A protein levels were lower in CRC tissues than in the nearby non-tumour tissues as shown by IHC staining.
source: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining of the cancer-adjacent borders of two patients showed that CPT1A protein levels were lower in CRC tissues than in the nearby non-tumour tissues (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Low CPT1A-expressing patients had low overall survival.
source: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis indicated that low CPT1A-expressing patients had low overall survival (OS) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: READ patients with low CPT1A had low overall survival with p=0.061.
source: Survival analysis of READ patients with low CPT1A using GEPIA also suggested a low OS; the difference was statistically close but not significant (p=0.061, Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by GEPIA survival analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: Patients with TRG score of 1 often have high IHC score for CPT1A.
source: Among patients with a tumour regression grade (TRG) score of 1, which indicates a minimal number of residual tumour cells, a high IHC score for CPT1A is often observed.
evidence: Supported by IHC scoring data from patient samples

claim: Patients with TRG score of 2 exhibited relatively lower IHC staining intensity and overall scores for CPT1A.
source: Conversely, patients with a TRG score of 2, indicating more residual tumour cells, exhibited relatively lower IHC staining intensity and overall scores (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 2D

claim: IHC scores were significantly higher in the TRG 1 group compared to TRG 2-3 group.
source: A comparison of groups with TRG 2–3 and TRG 1 revealed significantly higher IHC scores in the TRG 1 group (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by comparative IHC scoring data shown in Figure 2E

claim: TRG and IHC scores for CPT1A showed a negative correlation (R=−0.3430 and p=0.024).
source: The TRG and IHC scores for CPT1A showed a negative correlation (R=−0.3430 and p=0.024) (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2F

claim: SW480, Caco-2, SW620, HT-29 cells were more resistant to radiation than HCT15, RKO, and HCT 116 cells.
source: Through a colony formation assay (CFA) and multi-target single-hit survival model, we found that SW480, Caco-2, SW620, HT-29, and cells were more resistant to radiation than HCT15, RKO, and HCT 116 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by CFA and survival model data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: CPT1A transcription and protein levels were higher in radiation-resistant cells than in radiosensitive cells.
source: Furthermore, the background expression levels of CPT1A in the above cells revealed that CPT1A transcription and protein levels were higher in radiation-resistant cells than in radiosensitive cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: CPT1A knockout increased radioresistance in HCT116 cells (D0=1.526 vs 1.993, p<0.05).
source: The CFA and multi-target single-hit survival model suggested that radioresistance increased with CPT1A knockout (D0=1.526 vs 1.993, p<0.05, Figure 3C and D)
evidence: Supported by CFA and survival model data shown in Figure 3C and D

claim: CPT1A overexpression decreased radioresistance in SW480 cells (D0=2.724 vs 1.963, p<0.01).
source: whereas the radioresistance of cells decreased with CPT1A overexpression (D0=2.724 vs 1.963, p<0.01, Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Supported by CFA and survival model data shown in Figure 3E and F

claim: CPT1A knockout improved DNA damage repair as shown by decreased proportion of DNA in the tail of cells in comet assay.
source: The comet assay suggested that the proportion of DNA in the tail of cells decreased with CPT1A knockout, indicating improved damage repair.
evidence: Supported by comet assay data

claim: CPT1A overexpression reduced DNA damage repair capabilities as shown by increased proportion of DNA in the tail in comet assay.
source: With CPT1A overexpression, the proportion of DNA in the tail increased, indicating reduced damage repair capabilities (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by comet assay data shown in Figure 3G

claim: CPT1A knockout resulted in faster disappearance of γ-H2A.X from cells after 6 Gy irradiation, indicating improved cell damage repair.
source: We also detected γ-H2A.X expression at different time points after 6 Gy irradiation; with CPT1A knockout, γ-H2A.X disappeared from cells faster, indicating improved cell damage repair (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by γ-H2A.X expression data shown in Figure 3H

claim: CPT1A overexpression resulted in slower disappearance of γ-H2A.X in cells, remaining detectable even after 24 hr, indicating diminished cellular repair capability.
source: With CPT1A overexpression, the disappearance rate of γ-H2A.X in cells was slower, remaining detectable even after 24 hr, indicating diminished cellular repair capability (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by γ-H2A.X expression data shown in Figure 3I

claim: CPT1A knockout increased tumour weights in mice xenograft model, which persisted after radiotherapy.
source: CPT1A-stabilising knockout increased tumour weights in mice, which persisted after radiotherapy (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by xenograft tumor weight data shown in Figure 4B

claim: CPT1A knockout increased Ki-67 staining intensity and percentage of positive cells in xenograft tumours.
source: IHC staining demonstrated a significant increase in Ki-67 staining intensity and the percentage of positive cells in CPT1A knockout tumours, indicating enhanced proliferative capacity that was further pronounced after radiotherapy (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: In the absence of CPT1A knockdown, radiotherapy reduced the percentage of Ki67-positive cells in xenograft tumours by 32.9%.
source: In the absence of CPT1A knockdown, radiotherapy reduced the percentage of Ki67-positive cells in the xenograft tumours by 32.9% (approximately 39.6% of the pre-irradiation baseline).
evidence: Supported by quantitative IHC analysis

claim: Upon CPT1A knockdown, radiotherapy only led to a 14.5% reduction in the percentage of Ki67-positive cells.
source: In contrast, upon CPT1A knockdown, radiotherapy only led to a 14.5% reduction in the percentage of Ki67-positive cells (approximately 15.6% of the pre-irradiation baseline; Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative IHC analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: CPT1A overexpression resulted in reduced tumour weight in SW480 xenograft mice.
source: CPT1A overexpression resulted in reduced tumour weight in mice, a trend that persisted even after radiotherapy (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by xenograft tumor weight data shown in Figure 4F

claim: In the absence of CPT1A overexpression, radiotherapy resulted in a 0.10 g decrease in tumour weight (approximately 52.5% of the pre-irradiation weight).
source: Furthermore, as illustrated in Figure 4E and F, in the absence of CPT1A overexpression, radiotherapy resulted in a 0.10 g decrease in tumour weight (approximately 52.5% of the pre-irradiation weight)
evidence: Supported by tumor weight measurements shown in Figure 4E and F

claim: With CPT1A overexpression, radiotherapy induced a 0.12 g reduction in tumour weight (approximately 89.7% of the pre-irradiation weight).
source: whereas with CPT1A overexpression, radiotherapy induced a more pronounced 0.12 g reduction in tumour weight (approximately 89.7% of the pre-irradiation weight).
evidence: Supported by tumor weight measurements

claim: CPT1A overexpression decreased Ki-67 staining intensity and percentage of positive cells in xenograft tumours.
source: IHC staining for Ki-67 revealed significantly decreased staining intensity and percentage of positive cells in CPT1A-overexpressing tumours, indicating weakened proliferative capacity, which was further accentuated after radiotherapy (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4G and H

claim: With CPT1A knockdown, 363 genes were upregulated and 1290 genes were downregulated (|log2(fold change)|>1 and q<0.05).
source: With CPT1A knockdown, we found 363 upregulated and 1290 downregulated genes (|log2(fold change)|>1 and q<0.05) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Peroxisomes, cell cycle nucleotide excision repair, and fatty acid degradation pathways were among the enriched KEGG pathways in CPT1A knockdown cells.
source: We conducted Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis and Gene Ontology (GO) annotation for all differentially expressed genes (DEGs; Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E), showing that the peroxisomes, cell cycle nucleotide excision repair, and fatty acid degradation pathways were among the enriched KEGG pathways (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: Total ROS levels in CPT1A knockout cells decreased.
source: The total ROS levels in CPT1A knockout cells decreased, whereas those in CPT1A-overexpressing cells increased (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by ROS detection data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Total ROS levels in CPT1A-overexpressing cells increased.
source: The total ROS levels in CPT1A knockout cells decreased, whereas those in CPT1A-overexpressing cells increased (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by ROS detection data shown in Figure 5D

claim: In CPT1A knockout cells, the GSH/GSSG ratio increased.
source: in CPT1A knockout cells, the GSH/GSSG ratio and SOD and CAT enzyme activities increased, and these changes were also observed under 6 Gy irradiation (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by GSH/GSSG ratio measurements shown in Figure 5E

claim: In CPT1A knockout cells, SOD enzyme activity increased.
source: in CPT1A knockout cells, the GSH/GSSG ratio and SOD and CAT enzyme activities increased, and these changes were also observed under 6 Gy irradiation (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by SOD enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 5G

claim: In CPT1A knockout cells, CAT enzyme activity increased.
source: in CPT1A knockout cells, the GSH/GSSG ratio and SOD and CAT enzyme activities increased, and these changes were also observed under 6 Gy irradiation (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by CAT enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 5I

claim: In CPT1A-overexpressing cells, the GSH/GSSG ratio decreased.
source: In contrast, in CPT1A-overexpressing cells, the GSH/GSSG ratio, and SOD and CAT activities decreased, and these changes were also observed after 6 Gy irradiation (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by GSH/GSSG ratio measurements shown in Figure 5F

claim: In CPT1A-overexpressing cells, SOD enzyme activity decreased.
source: In contrast, in CPT1A-overexpressing cells, the GSH/GSSG ratio, and SOD and CAT activities decreased, and these changes were also observed after 6 Gy irradiation (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by SOD enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 5H

claim: In CPT1A-overexpressing cells, CAT enzyme activity decreased.
source: In contrast, in CPT1A-overexpressing cells, the GSH/GSSG ratio, and SOD and CAT activities decreased, and these changes were also observed after 6 Gy irradiation (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by CAT enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 5I

claim: CPT1A knockout in cells increased both the mRNA and protein levels of SOD1, SOD2, and CAT.
source: We examined the transcriptional and protein levels of SOD (SOD1, SOD2, and SOD3) and CAT (Figure 6A and B) and found that CPT1A knockout in cells increased both the mRNA and protein levels of SOD1, SOD2, and CAT
evidence: Supported by western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A and B

claim: CPT1A overexpression decreased the mRNA and protein levels of SOD1, SOD2, and CAT.
source: whereas the overexpression of CPT1A decreased them (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A and B

claim: FOXM1, LMNB1, and SAP30 are predicted transcription factors that regulate SOD1, SOD2, and CAT and are upregulated in CPT1A knockout cells.
source: Thus, we employed a bioinformatics analysis by intersecting predicted or reported transcription factors known to regulate SOD1, SOD2, and CAT with upregulated DEGs. The Venn diagram highlights three transcription factors that met the criteria: FOXM1, LMNB1, and SAP30 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: FOXM1 transcription and protein levels were significantly increased in CPT1A knockout cells.
source: FOXM1 transcription and protein levels were significantly increased in CPT1A knockout cells but decreased when CPT1A was overexpressed (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A and B

claim: FOXM1 transcription and protein levels decreased when CPT1A was overexpressed.
source: FOXM1 transcription and protein levels were significantly increased in CPT1A knockout cells but decreased when CPT1A was overexpressed (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A and B

claim: FOXM1 overexpression restored downstream SOD1, SOD2, and CAT protein levels in HCT 116-KO cells.
source: Finally, a rescue experiment was conducted by overexpressing FOXM1 in HCT 116-NC and HCT 116-KO cells, demonstrating that downstream SOD1, SOD2, and CAT protein levels were restored by FOXM1 overexpression (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6D

claim: FOXM1 positively correlates with SOD1 in READ and COAD.
source: Additionally, we explored the correlation between FOXM1 and the downstream enzymes SOD1, SOD2, and CAT in READ and COAD. The results (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B) indicate a positive correlation between FOXM1 and SOD1 as well as SOD2.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: FOXM1 positively correlates with SOD2 in READ and COAD.
source: Additionally, we explored the correlation between FOXM1 and the downstream enzymes SOD1, SOD2, and CAT in READ and COAD. The results (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B) indicate a positive correlation between FOXM1 and SOD1 as well as SOD2.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: The downregulation of CPT1A increases FOXM1 mRNA and protein levels in CRC, promoting the transcription and translation of SOD1, SOD2, and CAT.
source: In summary, the downregulation of CPT1A increases FOXM1 mRNA and protein levels in CRC, promoting the transcription and translation of SOD1, SOD2, and CAT, thereby accelerating the scavenging of ROS produced after radiation exposure and ultimately leading to radiation resistance in CRC cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental data and summarized in Figure 6E

claim: CPT1A downregulation accelerates the scavenging of ROS produced after radiation exposure.
source: In summary, the downregulation of CPT1A increases FOXM1 mRNA and protein levels in CRC, promoting the transcription and translation of SOD1, SOD2, and CAT, thereby accelerating the scavenging of ROS produced after radiation exposure and ultimately leading to radiation resistance in CRC cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by ROS detection and enzyme activity data

claim: CPT1A downregulation leads to radiation resistance in CRC cells.
source: In summary, the downregulation of CPT1A increases FOXM1 mRNA and protein levels in CRC, promoting the transcription and translation of SOD1, SOD2, and CAT, thereby accelerating the scavenging of ROS produced after radiation exposure and ultimately leading to radiation resistance in CRC cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assays, in vivo experiments, and mechanistic studies

claim: CPT1A was significantly downregulated in CRC.
source: CPT1A was significantly downregulated in CRC and negatively correlated with responsiveness to neoadjuvant radiotherapy.
evidence: Supported by multiple expression analyses from GEO, TCGA, qRT-PCR, western blot, and IHC

claim: CPT1A was negatively correlated with responsiveness to neoadjuvant radiotherapy.
source: CPT1A was significantly downregulated in CRC and negatively correlated with responsiveness to neoadjuvant radiotherapy.
evidence: Supported by TRG scoring and correlation analysis

claim: CPT1A mediates radiosensitivity, influencing reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging and DNA damage response.
source: Functional studies suggested that CPT1A mediates radiosensitivity, influencing reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging and DNA damage response.
evidence: Supported by functional studies including ROS detection, enzyme activity assays, and DNA damage assays

claim: CPT1A downregulates the FOXM1-SOD1/SOD2/CAT axis.
source: Mechanistic exploration revealed that CPT1A downregulates the FOXM1-SOD1/SOD2/CAT axis, moderating cellular ROS levels after irradiation and enhancing radiosensitivity.
evidence: Supported by western blot, qRT-PCR, and rescue experiments

claim: CPT1A moderates cellular ROS levels after irradiation.
source: Mechanistic exploration revealed that CPT1A downregulates the FOXM1-SOD1/SOD2/CAT axis, moderating cellular ROS levels after irradiation and enhancing radiosensitivity.
evidence: Supported by ROS detection experiments

claim: CPT1A enhances radiosensitivity.
source: Mechanistic exploration revealed that CPT1A downregulates the FOXM1-SOD1/SOD2/CAT axis, moderating cellular ROS levels after irradiation and enhancing radiosensitivity.
evidence: Supported by colony formation assays and in vivo experiments

claim: CPT1A downregulation contributes to radioresistance in CRC by augmenting the FOXM1-mediated antioxidant response.
source: CPT1A downregulation contributes to radioresistance in CRC by augmenting the FOXM1-mediated antioxidant response.
evidence: Supported by comprehensive mechanistic studies

claim: CPT1A is a potential biomarker of radiosensitivity.
source: Thus, CPT1A is a potential biomarker of radiosensitivity and a novel target for overcoming radioresistance, offering a future direction to enhance CRC radiotherapy.
evidence: Inferred from correlation with TRG scores and survival data

claim: CPT1A is a novel target for overcoming radioresistance.
source: Thus, CPT1A is a potential biomarker of radiosensitivity and a novel target for overcoming radioresistance, offering a future direction to enhance CRC radiotherapy.
evidence: Inferred from functional studies showing CPT1A modulates radiosensitivity

claim: Total ROS significantly reduced in radioresistant cells compared to HCT-15 control cells following 6 Gy irradiation.
source: Total ROS significantly reduced in radioresistant cells compared to those in HCT-15 control cells following 6 Gy irradiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and C).
evidence: Supported by ROS detection data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and C

claim: CPT1A overexpression increased total ROS levels in radioresistant cells.
source: Furthermore, CPT1A overexpression increased total ROS levels in radioresistant cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and D)
evidence: Supported by ROS detection data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and D

claim: Radioresistant cells showed increased GSH/GSSG ratio compared to parental HCT-15 control cells.
source: Additionally, we assessed the GSH/GSSG ratio (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F) and SOD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G and H), POD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2I and J), and CAT enzyme activities (Figure 5—figure supplement 2K) in radioresistant cells, both at baseline and after 6 Gy irradiation, revealing an increased GSH/GSSG ratio and elevated activities of SOD, POD, and CAT enzymes in radioresistant cells compared to those in parental HCT-15 control cells.
evidence: Supported by GSH/GSSG ratio measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F

claim: Radioresistant cells showed elevated activities of SOD, POD, and CAT enzymes compared to parental HCT-15 control cells.
source: Additionally, we assessed the GSH/GSSG ratio (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F) and SOD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G and H), POD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2I and J), and CAT enzyme activities (Figure 5—figure supplement 2K) in radioresistant cells, both at baseline and after 6 Gy irradiation, revealing an increased GSH/GSSG ratio and elevated activities of SOD, POD, and CAT enzymes in radioresistant cells compared to those in parental HCT-15 control cells.
evidence: Supported by enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2G-K

claim: CPT1A overexpression restored the GSH/GSSG ratio in HCT-15-25F-OE cells.
source: To explore the influence of CPT1A overexpression on radiation resistance, we examined the GSH/GSSG ratio (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F) and SOD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G and H), POD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2I and J), and CAT enzyme activities (Figure 5—figure supplement 2K) in HCT-15-25F-OE cells compared to those in control cells, showing that CPT1A overexpression restored the GSH/GSSG ratio and increased SOD and CAT enzyme activities but failed to restore POD enzyme activity.
evidence: Supported by GSH/GSSG ratio measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F

claim: CPT1A overexpression increased SOD enzyme activity in HCT-15-25F-OE cells.
source: To explore the influence of CPT1A overexpression on radiation resistance, we examined the GSH/GSSG ratio (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F) and SOD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G and H), POD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2I and J), and CAT enzyme activities (Figure 5—figure supplement 2K) in HCT-15-25F-OE cells compared to those in control cells, showing that CPT1A overexpression restored the GSH/GSSG ratio and increased SOD and CAT enzyme activities but failed to restore POD enzyme activity.
evidence: Supported by SOD enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2G and H

claim: CPT1A overexpression increased CAT enzyme activity in HCT-15-25F-OE cells.
source: To explore the influence of CPT1A overexpression on radiation resistance, we examined the GSH/GSSG ratio (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F) and SOD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G and H), POD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2I and J), and CAT enzyme activities (Figure 5—figure supplement 2K) in HCT-15-25F-OE cells compared to those in control cells, showing that CPT1A overexpression restored the GSH/GSSG ratio and increased SOD and CAT enzyme activities but failed to restore POD enzyme activity.
evidence: Supported by CAT enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2K

claim: CPT1A overexpression failed to restore POD enzyme activity in HCT-15-25F-OE cells.
source: To explore the influence of CPT1A overexpression on radiation resistance, we examined the GSH/GSSG ratio (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F) and SOD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G and H), POD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2I and J), and CAT enzyme activities (Figure 5—figure supplement 2K) in HCT-15-25F-OE cells compared to those in control cells, showing that CPT1A overexpression restored the GSH/GSSG ratio and increased SOD and CAT enzyme activities but failed to restore POD enzyme activity.
evidence: Supported by POD enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2I and J

claim: CPT1A overexpression increased the radiosensitivity of radioresistant cells (D0=2.871 vs 2.581, p<0.05).
source: CFAs and the multi-target single-hit survival model revealed that CPT1A overexpression increased the radiosensitivity of radioresistant cells (D0=2.871 vs 2.581, p<0.05; Figure 3—figure supplement 2G and H)
evidence: Supported by CFA and survival model data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G and H

claim: HCT-15-25F and HCT-15-5F cells showed increased radioresistance compared to parental HCT-15 cells.
source: Using CFAs and the multi-target single-hit survival model, we observed increased radioresistance in these new cell lines, as indicated by higher D0 values than those of the parental cells (HCT-15 D0=2.957, HCT-15-5F D0=3.240, HCT-15-25F D0=3.822) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by CFA and survival model data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C

claim: CPT1A protein expression was significantly decreased in HCT-15-25F and HCT-15-5F cells compared with the original cells.
source: We also found significantly decreased CPT1A protein expression in HCT-15-25F and HCT-15-5F cells compared with that in the original cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D

claim: CPT1A overexpression resulted in a slow disappearance of intracellular γ-H2A.X in HCT-15-25F cells.
source: To assess the impact of CPT1A overexpression on DNA repair capacity, we monitored γ-H2A.X expression at different time points following 6 Gy irradiation. CPT1A overexpression resulted in a slow disappearance of intracellular γ-H2A.X, suggesting enhanced DNA damage repair capability (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by γ-H2A.X expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F

claim: FOXM1 has potential binding sites in the promoters of SOD1, SOD2, and CAT as predicted by hTFtarget and JASPAR.
source: Furthermore, we used hTFtarget and JASPAR to predict FOXM1 binding sites in the promoters of SOD1, SOD2, and CAT (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics prediction using hTFtarget and JASPAR databases
